title: Preparing MPs and their offices for a post-election surge
label: 20 October 2026 · General Election Planning
summary: The panel from IPSA (Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority) and the House’s Members’ HR team reviewed how they supported MPs through the big turnover after the 2024 election. They said planning from late 2023, repurposing staff, named account managers, a cash advance and extended winding-up helped, but finding constituency offices, doing lease due diligence, getting London accommodation, recruiting trusted staff and handling equipment and FOI pressures remain tricky. They described pilots (IPSA-held leases, a pool of vetted temporary caseworkers, inter-office staff loans) and suggested clearer milestones, earlier candidate guidance and centralised services for the next election.

chapters.title: How IPSA and the House responded to 2024
chapters.takeaway: IPSA started planning in late 2023, repurposed staff into election roles, and provided tailored support for new, returning and departing MPs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You told us your 2024 response was your most successful. What made it work?

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We planned from late 2023, reused our existing staff in election roles rather than hiring surge workers, learned from past elections, and gave tailored support to new, returning and departing MPs.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We gave every new MP a named account manager, offered a cash advance option, phased onboarding, more induction, and worked closely with House services to be joined-up.

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: That agility helped us handle a record turnover: 350 MPs changed and 51% were first-time MPs.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: Our post-election survey showed mixed but generally positive feedback: about 45% rated support highly, some rated it lower, and 23% didn’t answer.

chapters.title: Finding and running constituency offices
chapters.takeaway: Securing offices is one of the hardest tasks; IPSA is trialling holding leases to reduce the burden but due diligence and timing create challenges.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Many new MPs found setting up constituency offices overwhelming. How can IPSA simplify that?

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: We’ve simplified the property-registration process and shifted responsibility from a central property team to individual account managers to speed things up and give direct support.

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: We’re trialling IPSA taking on leases: we’ve signed two leases so far and have five in the pipeline—this removes the admin burden for MPs.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: Why is IPSA’s lease due diligence challenging?

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: Because IPSA must survey buildings, pay legal fees and negotiate right-to-occupy terms—it’s more resource-intensive than an MP signing their own lease, but it protects staff and public money.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: Is IPSA lowering standards for MPs who take their own leases?

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: No. Our aim is to help MPs conduct proper checks or take the lease on their behalf so staff have safe premises.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could IPSA keep a list of available offices and offer turnkey handovers from departing MPs?

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: Yes—we’re asking for two-month break clauses on leases and want to create property lists so a new MP can choose to take an existing secure, equipped office or have IPSA hold the lease.

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: Boundary changes complicate this: some offices won’t suit every incoming MP, but a handover option could save time and public money.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: Dilapidations after the 2024 election cost over £1 million. Being leaseholder would reduce those handover costs in future.

chapters.title: Money, London accommodation and early logistics
chapters.takeaway: IPSA provided a £2,000 cash advance and faster access to payment cards and pre-booked hotels; it’s centralising services to avoid MPs fronting costs.

turns.speaker: Mary Glindon
turns.text: Some new MPs had tax and student loan surprises—how will you inform candidates pre-election?

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: We can work with parties, the House and HMRC to give clearer, general information to candidates about personal tax implications of becoming an MP.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We offered a £2,000 cash advance in 2024—124 MPs used it—deducted from their first salary. That helped people who’d spent money campaigning.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We also issued payment cards within two weeks and pre-booked hotels through the Travel Office so MPs didn’t have to pay up front; the Travel Office now pays hotels directly.

turns.speaker: Alberto Costa
turns.text: Could IPSA arrange family-friendly London accommodation beyond hotel rooms?

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: Yes. We capture MPs’ needs and can broaden bookings to apartments. We’re also exploring whether IPSA could hold London leases, though personal arrangements make that trickier.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We’re centralising services—broadband, utilities, stationery—so MPs don’t have to use personal funds and claim back later.

turns.speaker: Mary Glindon
turns.text: Could the cash advance be larger or repaid over a longer time?

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We’ll review whether £2,000 was enough and whether repayment terms should change, balancing support for MPs with responsible use of public money.

chapters.title: Recruiting staff, temporary support and training
chapters.takeaway: Given the surge of new MPs, the House runs HR guidance and IPSA pilots a vetted pool of temporary caseworkers and inter-office staff loans to speed office readiness.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: Recruiting staff fast was a top worry. What help did you offer?

turns.speaker: Kim McGrath
turns.text: We had best-practice recruitment guides, in-party sessions warning MPs not to rush hiring, dedicated HR drop-ins during induction, and an HR room at Portcullis House staffed by advisers.

turns.speaker: Kim McGrath
turns.text: Cases handled by Members’ HR doubled after the election—going from about 175 to 350 a month—and have since climbed as MPs seek help early.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: Could a temporary pool of vetted staff help with email and casework before MPs get full teams?

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: Yes—we’re piloting a pool of trained, vetted caseworkers tied to the staffing support fund. We’ve hired partners to build that pipeline so people are ready at the next election.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We also run an inter-office staff loan scheme letting departing MPs’ experienced staff temporarily work for new MPs, which helps continuity for constituents.

turns.speaker: Kim McGrath
turns.text: We advise new MPs to recruit an office manager first—the best single step to avoid early chaos—and we plan to give candidates HR guidance earlier, even before elections.

turns.speaker: Kim McGrath
turns.text: We’re publishing a recruitment booklet for new MPs and will hand it to everyone entering Parliament or at by-elections.

chapters.title: Winding up, equipment and public scrutiny
chapters.takeaway: IPSA extended the winding-up to four months and paid a four-month loss-of-office sum to departing MPs, but equipment rules, lease timings and FOI/press handling need clearer guidance and milestones.

turns.speaker: Bambos Charalambous
turns.text: How did you change the winding-up process and loss-of-office payments?

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: We extended the winding-up period to four months and had an experienced account manager team supporting departing MPs through redundancy, property exits and finance.

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We also paid the winding-up/loss-of-office payment—equal to four months’ salary—to departing MPs, including those who stood down or lost their seat, mostly paid by end of October 2024.

turns.speaker: Bambos Charalambous
turns.text: Some departing MPs said equipment was thrown away instead of being allowed to buy it. Why are rules restrictive?

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: There are different rules: IPSA-funded equipment can be kept for a fee or donated, but parliamentary equipment that connects to Parliament’s network can’t be reissued for security reasons. PDS now supplies more kit, which clarifies the process.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: Could House devices be wiped so MPs could buy them?

turns.speaker: Kim McGrath
turns.text: Technically possible but it costs a few hundred pounds per item; colleagues in digital services would need to weigh security, cost and public value.

turns.speaker: Mr Barros-Curtis
turns.text: New MPs also face FOIs and public scrutiny on expenses. Can IPSA change tone and context in its publications to reduce misuse and help MPs cope?

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: Yes. We’re consulting on transparency and plan clearer context-setting material—such as a booklet on what IPSA funds—to explain staffing costs and counter misleading summaries. We will support MPs facing malicious FOIs or press attacks.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: Many departing MPs delayed clearing offices and that blocked rooms for new MPs. Could we reinstate a packing-up system so offices can be cleared quickly after an election?

turns.speaker: Kim McGrath
turns.text: I know there’s a five working-day requirement to clear offices; the House manages the practical detail. I’ll try to follow up on clearance statistics so the Committee can look at it.

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: We learned some departing MPs used the full four months, which delayed handovers; next time we want clearer milestones and lease planning to speed transitions.

chapters.title: Next steps and unresolved issues
chapters.takeaway: IPSA and the House will expand pilots (leases, staff pools), improve candidate guidance, centralise more services and refine transparency and equipment rules before the next general election.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To wrap up: what are the concrete steps you’ll take before the next election?

turns.speaker: Karen Walker
turns.text: We’ll expand the lease trial, centralise more services so MPs don’t front costs, pilot the vetted caseworker pool, refine the cash-advance and repayment terms, and improve transparency materials for FOIs and press context.

turns.speaker: Karen Lacey
turns.text: We’ll create lists of available constituency offices for handovers, simplify property forms, set clearer winding-up milestones and continue to support departing staff’s employability.

turns.speaker: Kim McGrath
turns.text: We’ll publish and distribute a recruitment guide earlier, deliver more candidate briefings about employer responsibilities, and keep building HR support and training for staff transitions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks to all three of you for practical, evidence-based answers. We’ll follow up on office-clearance timings and take this into our next session.
